tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Silk Road, one of the greatest trade networks in history. The main routes were more than six thousand kilometres long.

The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian travelled west around one hundred and thirty BC and helped to open the routes. Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, became rich and famous centres of trade.

Besides silk, merchants carried spices, paper, glass and precious stones, and also ideas and religions. The routes became less important when sea trade grew cheaper in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

tx.t: Today I would like to outline what glaciers are, and why they matter for sea level. Glaciers cover about ten per cent of the world's land area.
Together, glaciers and ice sheets store about two thirds of the world's fresh water. A glacier forms when snow builds up for many years and is pressed into dense ice.
Since nineteen hundred, the global sea level has risen by about twenty centimetres. This rise is caused partly by melting ice and partly because warm water takes up more space.

The scheme soon met a serious problem: too few bikes in the hills. The council solved it with a van that moves bikes uphill every morning.
Today, a ride costs one pounds five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.
A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

The main reason for the decline was water pollution from farms. So volunteers and rangers fenced the river banks and cleaned the water.
By twenty thirteen, the number had risen to one hundred and twenty-five pairs, which shows that careful management can work.

tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.
Rapid growth can cause housing shortages, traffic jams and air pollution. Some cities are planting trees and building cycle lanes to make urban life healthier.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Ashby. It began in twenty fifteen with six hundred and twenty-three bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by fifty-eight per cent, and on a busy day there were more than five thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: theft and damage. The council solved it with a tracking system fixed inside each frame.
Today, a ride costs two pounds ninety-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.
